ratings.comment: Humidity-based auto-cutoff removes the need to choose a time and is technically proven in sensor-cook models, though it is not very radical.
An outcome-based 'heat to eating temperature' control is intuitive, but IR only reads the surface and the metal-free cavity adds complexity.
Very simple and easy to build, but fixed presets are common and not radical; it also keeps the power knob, which undercuts the simplicity.
Quirky and tangible, but tokens can get lost and add a step, so it is not simpler than a dial.
A pull-cord is a playful, numberless interface, but it is imprecise and not obviously easier than a dial.
A single-purpose mug cavity removes all configuration and is easy to build, but its narrow use limits how widely it serves the need, and it is a modest substitution.
A pictogram cam dial is cheap and intuitive, but icon-based presets already exist on many microwaves, so it is not radical.
Offline keyword voice control is plausible and needs no learning, but it is vague about how it knows food quantity, and speech recognition adds cost and can fail.
Scanning the package barcode removes the need to read instructions, but it needs a database of cooking times and does not work for food without a barcode, such as leftovers.

A bimetal thermostat that replaces the timer is a radical and cheap substitution, but exhaust air temperature is an unreliable proxy for doneness and the approach risks overheating or underheating the food.
Hold-to-heat is very simple and intuitive, though the clockwork timer adds a redundant element and holding a button for minutes is tiring.
A pedal is a familiar metaphor and keeps hands free, but it needs floor space, and variable power by pressure is unclear and hardly simpler.
A visible hourglass is a whimsical, intuitive timer, but fixed durations limit it and the optical sensing adds complexity.
Removing the start step is the most direct route to no learning curve, though a fixed 60 s is inflexible and the reversal of normal safety logic needs care.
Mass-based auto time requires no input, but weight is a poor proxy for the heating needed and the mechanical cam would be hard to make accurate.
A transparent mesh cavity adds visibility but does not simplify operation, and it contradicts its own title by keeping the lamp; it is also hard to build robustly.
The toaster lever is a familiar gesture, but a top-loading cavity with a choke seal is hard to make safe and it limits which dishes fit.
A drawer that starts when pushed closed is plausible and removes steps, but the cook time is still unspecified and drawer microwaves already exist.
A twist egg timer as the sole control closely mirrors old mechanical microwave dials, so it is very simple and cheap, though not very radical.
Dish-embedded RFID presets make cooking zero-input, but they lock users into branded cookware and cover limited cases.
Whimsical and novel, but a water-based timer in a microwave is messy, imprecise and arguably harder to use than a dial.
Removing the panel simplifies the look, but a single button leaves duration and power unresolved and a transparent front is vague.
A saucepan-like lid is a familiar metaphor, but RF sealing and safety interlocks without a latch are hard, and it does not simplify the controls.
A single large detented knob with raised icons is directly learnable by feel and easy to build, though not very radical.
Fixing a single gentle power level removes the hardest concept and is feasible, but slower heating is a trade-off.
A slider is easier to grasp than numbered steps, but it is an incremental change and still leaves a separate time control.
One dial for time and power cuts the controls in half, though coupling the two limits flexibility and some foods will heat badly.
Removing timing decisions entirely would give zero learning curve, but a camera classifier in a hot, steamy cavity is hard to make reliable and adds cost.
Acoustic popcorn detection is plausible and proven, but it covers only a narrow set of foods, so it helps ease of use only a little.
A burnable fuse strip is wild and memorable, but a combustible inside a microwave is dangerous, and it adds consumables and hassle.
Voice bell is easy and clearer than a beep, but it only helps at the end of the cycle and is an incremental swap.
A passive thermochromic door panel is a clever, cheap state indicator, but it shows heat rather than operation, and the door glass must also keep the microwave shielding.
A mode stirrer is a real, existing substitute for a turntable and removes a setup error, but it barely affects how the user operates the microwave and may heat less evenly.
Auto-start on load and door close removes all controls, but a fixed 90 s cycle and the risk of accidental or unsafe starts (empty cavity, wrong food) limit it.
A phone-only interface is technically easy, but it adds pairing and app steps, which works against the no-learning-curve need.
Radical single-affordance concept that removes learning, but it only fits flat plates, the eject mechanism is unclear, and it is hard to substitute for a cavity and door safely.
Cheap and practical, but it still needs a chart to be read and a knob to be set, so it only partly removes the learning curve.
Concrete as a part swap, but it does nothing for ease of operation, and lighting through the door glass is questionable.
A familiar external timer is simple to use, but a microwave that is always on is a safety problem, and it needs a door interlock and power-level control.
The visible time-left ribbon is intuitive and tangible, but it adds mechanical complexity and does little to simplify setting the time.

A spring-loaded auto-open door is already standard on most microwaves (the open button), so it's easy to build and gives a clear 'done' signal. It does little to simplify the input side of operation, and it isn't radical, because it replaces the bell with something similar rather than rethinking the controls.
Merging loading and timer setting is intuitive, but door angle as a timer input is awkward and hard to make precise, and the door interlock safety design adds complexity.
Tilting a heavy appliance is impractical and unsafe, and a pendulum timer is a weak fit; the gesture is not intuitive for setting time.
A visual done-ness cue is simple, but a sticker on a turntable edge reads the plate rather than the food, and the user must still decide when to stop.
A kettle-style single rocker is very easy to use and cheap, but it is not a radical idea and needs some auto-termination logic, such as a sensor or a fixed time.
A periscope mirror is a cheap substitution for the window, but it does little for operation simplicity and the mirrors could get dirty or heat-damaged.
A rotary dial is intuitive and self-starting, feasible with a mechanical spring and escapement, though dialing a single digit of minutes limits flexibility.
Word-labelled caps that mechanically limit the knob range are simple and understandable, but the caps are somewhat incremental and preset-dependent.
A zero-control blind oven removes learning entirely, but reliably deciding cook time from weight and IR is hard, and removing the window and lamp undermines user trust and visibility.
A kettle whistle is a familiar cue, but microwaves produce little steam flow through the vent and it only replaces the done signal, not the operation.
A fixed 60-second push cam is very simple and feasible, but it is a modest and not very radical change, and it is inflexible for different foods.
A single button with IR sensing removes all settings, though judging the right time and power for varied foods is hard and the idea is somewhat expected.
A load-cell turntable is concrete and feasible, but weight alone is a crude proxy for heating needs and some food-type input may still be needed.
A transparent casing is only loosely tied to ease of operation, and RF shielding with fully transparent glass is difficult.
Hold-to-heat has no learning curve and is simple to build, but it is tiring for long heating and has safety and ergonomic drawbacks.
An hourglass is a familiar metaphor and easy to implement, but users still have to choose a duration, and the fixed sand time limits flexibility.
Zero-step operation that matches the need, but a fixed 60 s default risks accidental starts (e.g., running empty) and is inflexible beyond reheats.
Simple single gesture, though it needs a capacitive or vibration sensor on the front and tapping is slightly less discoverable than a door-close start.
Intuitive and easy to build, but food-icon presets already exist on many microwaves, so it is not radical.
Self-ending cycles remove time entry, but humidity-based stopping is inconsistent across foods and still needs a start action.
Removes settings for packaged meals, but it depends on packaging standards and does not cover non-packaged food, and scanning adds a step.
Offline voice commands remove the controls entirely and need no learning, but noise, accents and the limited command set are real weaknesses, and voice-controlled microwaves already exist.
A spring-loaded door pop gives a clear physical done signal, but it only helps at the end of the cycle and does nothing for setting up the cook.
A speech chip is cheap and easy to build, but it only clarifies the done signal and is an incremental change.
A stove-style dial uses a familiar mental model, but running with no timer risks overcooking and has safety and food-quality problems.
A retracting pull-cord makes time visible and intuitive and is quite radical, though the mechanism is awkward and imprecise and its reliability is questionable.
A single twist-and-push handle that opens, sets time and starts is simple and plausible, though a time dial still requires some thought.
A top-loading pot-style microwave is radical and intuitive, but it brings ergonomic, spillage and leakage-shielding challenges, and it doesn't say how time gets set.
Mode stirrers already exist, and removing the turntable helps cleaning more than operation, so its effect on the learning curve is marginal.
Three verb buttons make operation very simple, but presets are common and not very radical.
Targeting a temperature rather than a time matches user intent, but IR sensing only reads the surface and is affected by steam and containers.
Auto food recognition removes nearly all settings and learning, but it is unreliable on varied foods and the substitution framing is a stretch (adds components rather than simplifying).
Interesting substitution of the bulb, but it barely affects operation simplicity and electroluminescent enamel in a microwave cavity is implausible.
A shrinking LED bar is easy to build and intuitive for progress, though it covers only the display and not setting the time.
A sliding door makes opening obvious, but microwave seals and choke requirements make it harder, and it does not address operation of the controls.
A magnetic latch with a pull-anywhere door is simple and feasible, but it is a modest change that is similar to existing pull-handle designs.
Wave-per-minute counting is easy to build, but it assumes users know the gesture and it is hard to use for long cook times, so it is not truly zero-learning.
Choosing a bowl as the whole interface is intuitive, but it ties the user to proprietary dishes and limits flexibility, and it adds cost rather than cutting it.
A single touchpad is simple and cheap, but the x/y mapping to time and power must be learned and is imprecise.
Acoustic auto-stop removes the need to set a timer for popcorn and liquids, but it is unreliable for other foods and noisy in a real kitchen.
A two-way toggle is easy to understand and cheap to build, but the idea is incremental and limits control.
Outcome-based slider is very intuitive, but without sensing it is hard to map reliably to food types and quantities, and it is not very radical.
Radical and simple to use, but near-field phased pad heating with safe shielding is technically doubtful and the cloche leakage risk is high.
Easy and feasible, but it only improves completion feedback rather than operation, so the effect on the learning curve is modest.
Reduces parts but does almost nothing for user operation, and airflow-driven rotation is hard to make reliable under load.
Single-button force mapping is clever and buildable, but pressure levels are not self-evident and need learning and consistent force control.
Auto-detecting frozen food removes the need to know about defrost, though a floor thermistor may struggle to sense the load's temperature reliably.
A conveyor tunnel makes operation a single motion, but it faces serious challenges with RF leakage, size, cost and variable food loads.
An LED lamp swap is easy to build but barely touches the need for simple operation, and it is not radical.
A task dial with detents is intuitive and easy to build, but presets already exist and the dial still needs labels to be read.
A foot pedal is easy to grasp and feasible, but it only replaces the start button, leaving time and power unresolved, and it is awkward to use.
A roll-top shutter is a fresh swap for the hinged door, but sealing microwave leakage around a tambour is very hard and it does little for the learning curve.
Liners are feasible and simplify cleaning, but they have little to do with operation, and paper in a microwave raises safety concerns.
A physical mug cradle that triggers a program removes settings for a common task, though it only covers one use case.
Thermal sensing with automatic stop removes timer guessing, which fits zero learning curve well, though low-res IR through a microwave cavity is challenging.
A webcam and screen replace the window but add complexity and cost, and cameras in a hot, humid cavity are a problem, with little help for ease of use.

An RGB cavity light is cheap and technically easy, and it gives an intuitive ambient status cue. It only addresses feedback, though, not how to operate the microwave, and the cold/warm/hot colour mapping is not very radical or clearly tied to actual doneness.
A mechanical gravity timer with a visible countdown is intuitive and a cheap substitution for electronics, though the 'lid-weight' placement is a bit odd and time precision is limited.
Zero-input operation is appealing, but plate diameter is a poor proxy for food quantity or type, and a capacitive floor sensor under a turntable is questionable.
Simple and already common behavior, so it reduces the learning curve a little but is not radical or a true substitution.
Removing the power control simplifies operation sensibly, but the idea is incremental and relies on a load sensor to do the adaptive work.
A lid that senses temperature removes time-setting entirely and is intuitive, though a microwave-safe wireless temperature sensor is challenging and the lid is an extra part to supply.
A single button with automatic stop fully removes the learning curve, but IR surface sensing is unreliable for uneven or covered food.
Very simple and safe to build, but holding the paddle for minutes is tiring, and it is arguably a step backward.
The toaster metaphor is familiar, but it still needs a time setting, so it only partly removes the learning curve.
Easy to understand and cheap to build, but similar preset dials already exist, so it is not radical.
Weight-based automatic timing is plausible and removes the settings, but weight is a weak proxy for food type and starting temperature.
Humidity-sensor auto-stop already exists on sensor-cook microwaves, so it is a proven but not very radical way to remove timer guesswork.
Barcodes usually don't encode heating programs, so it needs a database or new packaging standard, but it removes all input for packaged food.
Containers carrying their own profile make for a novel zero-interface concept, but it requires an ecosystem of tagged containers and RFID inside a microwave cavity is difficult.
Offline keyword spotting is feasible, but voice still needs time or quantity input and noisy kitchens and discoverability limit the no-learning-curve claim.
A single 'how much' knob is simple, cheap and intuitive, though it is a modest simplification rather than a radical one.
A glanceable colour scale removes number estimation and is trivially cheap, but it is a modest rather than radical change.
Units that match what the user is heating remove translation effort, though the mapping from mugs to time is imprecise.
A two-way rocker is easy and clearer, but simplified power switches are already common.
Removing the power control cuts decisions to one, but it loses defrost and gentle heating, so it is not very radical.
Inverter technology is real and specific, but it is more complex and costly, and it is not a simplification of operation.
Solid-state RF with reflected-power feedback enables true auto-cook and no settings, though cost and power levels are still hurdles; it is not cheaper, so it fits SUBSTITUTE only loosely.
A cost-saving swap that does nothing for operation simplicity, and a non-resettable fuse can worsen the user experience.
Removing the stored-energy hazard is appealing but only tangentially related to ease of use, and a high-voltage magnetron supply without any storage capacitor is questionable.
Mode stirrers are well-established and remove the turntable hassle, giving modest simplicity gains.
Rotating antennas are already in commercial products; they remove the turntable seating error and ease cleaning.
Clever part substitution, but it does nothing for ease of operation, and fan airflow is unlikely to turn a loaded plate reliably.
Safer and easier to handle, but a floppy mat may not rotate well on the roller ring and the benefit to operation is marginal.
Plausible and practical for maintenance, but it is unrelated to operating the microwave without learning.
A magnetic pull-open door with Hall-sensor interlocks removes the button-finding step and is technically plausible, though safety certification of the interlocks needs care.
Highly intuitive and easy to build (some models already use it), but it is not radical.
Drawer gesture is intuitive and fairly radical, though RF choke on a sliding drawer and spill handling are tough; it also substitutes the door rather than just a part.
Hands-free opening is easy to implement with proven sensors, but accidental triggering is a risk and the benefit to learning curve is modest.
A mechanical shutter is a safety feature that is invisible to the user, so it does little for ease of operation and adds complexity.
A single hinge-contact interlock is unreliable and unsafe by regulation, and has little connection to the user's learning curve.
An optical seating sensor is plausible but only marginally reduces confusion; it is not a safe standalone monitor channel.
The mesh gasket is a manufacturing substitution, and its link to simpler operation is indirect, resting on a hoped-for better-labelled panel.
ITO glass is a named, concrete substitution, but ITO shielding at 2.45 GHz while staying transparent and surviving heat is doubtful, and visibility only modestly helps usability.
A fully see-through mesh cavity is radical, but it has serious problems with RF leakage, hygiene, and cleaning, and it only addresses feedback, not operation.
LED lighting is already common and barely touches the learning-curve need.
Colour status on the window is intuitive, feasible, and replaces the beep with a glanceable signal that needs no learning.
Talking microwaves already exist; it helps clarity but does not simplify operation or substitute much.
Touch-triggered spoken help removes the need for a manual, but the idea is fairly incremental and the speaker adds cost rather than substituting a part.
The pull-cord timer is a tactile, intuitive input that replaces the dial, though precision and retraction mechanics are a concern.
The visible sand timer is charming and number-free, but fixed durations limit flexibility and the sensor adds complexity.
The crank-wound clockwork and power cam is a playful metaphor and mechanically plausible, but the turns-to-power mapping is not obvious and the crank is effortful.
Very simple and practical, though similar to existing quick-start buttons, so not very radical.
Zero-setting operation is intuitive, but holding a button for minutes is tiring and not suited to elderly users.
Charming and intuitive, but flipping a glass and sand-sensing is unreliable, and fixed durations are imprecise.
Pouring water into an appliance next to a magnetron is messy and unsafe, and it adds steps instead of simplifying.
Pull-cord mechanical timer is intuitive with visible time and plausible, similar to old mechanical timers, though it needs a robust escapement.
A retractable cord eases setup but does nothing for operating the microwave, and it's an incremental, familiar mechanism.
A wall-hanging 300 W unit is odd and simplifies installation, but the weight, heat and socket load make it hard, and it barely addresses operation.
A USB-C solid-state mug heater is novel and has one-button simplicity, but 100 W RF over USB-C is weak and barely plausible for heating food.
Closing the door to start removes nearly all controls and learning, though it needs sensing of the load and raises safety and accidental-start concerns.
A single big knob is clear, easy to build and intuitive, though a simple control consolidation is not radical.
Very practical and simple to use, but a labelled detented knob is hardly radical and only covers a few presets.
Foot-pedal start is unusual and feasible, but it doesn't reduce the learning curve and adds hygiene and safety issues like accidental starts.
The camera with automatic boil-over detection is novel and reduces the need for technique, but cost, steam fogging and the added interface work against simplicity.
A nucleation stick is a cheap physical substitute for knowledge, but it only addresses superheating and the user must remember to use it.
An arc-detecting cutoff forgives the 'no metal' mistake and removes a rule to learn, but the liner and sensor details are vague and arcing detection is hard to make reliable.
Intuitive and easy to build, but it is still a manual timer with a different form factor, and it is not very radical.
Pictograms remove the number conversion and are easy to implement, but similar preset buttons are already common.
Zero-input operation is ideal, but weight is a poor proxy for the heating needed (food type, starting temperature), and the load cell must work in a microwave environment.
Humidity sensors for auto-cooking already exist and need no input, but they work poorly for foods that don't steam.
A warm/hot knob matches how people think, but an IR sensor only reads surface temperature and the cavity has to be designed around it, which limits reliability.
Removing the power knob does simplify operation and is easy to build, but a fixed 500 W setting limits versatility and is hardly radical.
A mechanical notched-card reader is a cheap substitute for the electronic panel and needs no learning, though it depends on cards being available.
Barcode scanning is feasible and removes manual entry, but it needs a database and only works for packaged food.
Placing the food is the whole interaction, which fits the need very well, but it requires tagged packaging and NFC reading inside a microwave cavity is hard.
Offline voice control is natural and workable, but it is common in existing products and raises noise and accent issues.
Touch-free wave-to-add-time is easy to grasp, but accidental triggers, no feedback on the total, and no power control limit its usefulness.
A single joystick is plausible and compact, but mapping axes to time and power is not intuitive and needs some learning.
Setting by quantity removes the abstract time and power decisions, and it is feasible with a lookup table, though food type still matters.
Counting turntable revolutions is a wild and visible progress cue, but 'turns' is no more intuitive than time and the rotation speed is variable.
A quartz timer is a sensible, feasible substitution, but it is nearly invisible to users and does little for the learning curve.
Removes all controls and fits the zero-learning-curve need, though an 8x8 thermopile sees only surface temperature through steam and a metal-mesh door, which makes accurate closed-loop control hard.
Very simple and easy to build, but a fixed 60 s dose is inflexible and needs repeated door cycling.
A cheap, plausible simplification, but it still leaves a control and a time setting to learn, so the gain is incremental.
The stove-knob metaphor is familiar, but inverter drives cost more than they save, which runs against SUBSTITUTE, and the dial still needs a time control.
Using shelf height for power is wild and removes the knob, but standing-wave hot spots make the effect unpredictable and the placement rule is less intuitive than it sounds.
Plausible cheap thermal timer that keeps the one-knob control, but it is not much simpler for the user and likely less accurate than the mechanical timers already in use.
Oil dashpot timers do exist and keep the familiar twist, but the user gets little new and accuracy and temperature drift are concerns.
Reusing a familiar egg timer is a clever way to avoid learning anything, but detecting the ring reliably and cutting power is clunky and unreliable.
Tokens give a tangible and wild way to set time that is easy to grasp, but they can be lost and make flexible timing harder.
Easy and cheap to build and it makes the end of the cycle clearer, but it only affects feedback and not operation, and it is hardly radical.
A lift-off magnetic door is novel and has no latch to learn, but it still leaves operation of the controls unaddressed, and the safety interlock and RF sealing are challenging.
Very feasible and familiar, but it is close to existing doors and only addresses opening, so it is not radical.
A drawer is intuitive and has some precedent in drawer microwaves, but the choke-rail shielding and the controls remain open issues.
Rice-cooker-style top loading is familiar, but cylindrical cavity heating and loading ergonomics are questionable and the idea says little about how to start or set it.
Merging start, timing and finish into one toaster-like motion directly removes the learning curve, though a mechanical timer and pop-up for varied foods are tricky.
Very radical doorless turret is intriguing, but RF sealing on a rotating drum and food spillage when rotating make it hard, and the single-motion benefit is only moderate.
Chain-mail curtain is novel and intuitive like a blind, but mesh gaps, leakage at edges, and cleaning are significant concerns.
Roll-up shutter is concrete and plausible with interlocking slats forming a choke, though it is bulky and less simple than a normal door.
Familiar oven-style door is highly intuitive with no learning curve and easily built, but it is hardly radical and the weight of a loaded door is a minor issue.
Foot pedal with Bowden cable is simple and practical for full hands, but it adds a hidden control to discover rather than removing learning.
Easy door-opening bar helps a bit, but only addresses door release, not operation overall, and is similar to existing push-bar designs.
Auto-opening door removes a step with a plausible capacitive sensor and solenoid, though it only covers the end-of-cycle opening.
Clever mechanical substitution where one cam both rings the bell and pops the door, giving an intuitive done signal, but it is limited to old timer-style units.
A simple gravity hook replaces the spring and button latch, but a lift-to-open action is not obviously more intuitive and the safety interlock needs care.
A clear window helps judge doneness, but it does little for operation simplicity, and transparent conductive coatings at microwave shielding levels are technically challenging.
A cheaper, lighter door is plausible, but it barely addresses zero-learning-curve operation, and a clear polymer with mesh must still shield microwaves while staying see-through.
A floppy door is a wild idea, but a conductive silicone hinge would struggle to seal against microwave leakage and to hold the interlock reliably, and it does little for operation simplicity.
A cover-to-heat cloche is a radical, intuitive interaction with essentially no learning curve, though shielding at the seam and controlling power need engineering.
Automatic hand-back removes the door-opening step and is concrete, but it ignores the start and setup controls and adds mechanical complexity and a leakage path through the flap.
A two-button fob is very simple and easy to build, but remote controls are a familiar idea, and a remote start raises safety concerns when nobody is watching the oven.

Removing timer-setting with a 'red means ready' cue strongly serves zero-learning-curve operation, but a thermochromic ring on the turntable reflects plate/surface temperature rather than food temperature, and the photodiode sensing and heat-resistant microwave-safe pigment add reliability doubts.
One-button heat-until-hot is ideal for zero learning, though IR surface sensing is unreliable for uneven food and a single button gives no control over different foods.
Weight-based timing removes user choice, but weight is a poor proxy for needed time, and the description is internally inconsistent (load cell vs. mechanical spring scale).
A familiar hourglass metaphor is quirky and clear, but the user still has to pick a duration and the glass fixes it to one time.
Pull-cord spring timer is simple, mechanical and cheap, though judging how far to pull still requires estimating a time.
The toaster lever is a universally understood interaction and mechanically plausible, though lever depth as time setting is imprecise.
A hold-to-run paddle removes all numbers and learning, and a dead-man switch is simple and safe, though holding it for minutes is tiring.
Icon-based dial with fixed cams is cheap and intuitive, but presets are less flexible and similar presets already exist.
A press-per-minute button with lamps is very easy to understand and mechanically simple, but it's close to existing quick-start buttons.
Needs no user input if it works, but it depends on packaging tags that don't exist and NFC reading inside a metal cavity is hard.
Counting turntable revolutions is highly original, but it is less intuitive than time and offers little real benefit.
Height-based power is novel but standing-wave hot spots make it unpredictable, and a raised shelf isn't self-explanatory to users.
A mechanical iris on the waveguide is a concrete way to get continuous power, though it risks magnetron mismatch and reflected power, and a slider still needs some user understanding.
The stove-flame analogy is intuitive, but a movable water load wastes energy and adds mess and complexity.
Two plain-language settings directly remove the learning curve and are easy to build, but the idea is not radical.
Removing the power control is the simplest possible operation, though one power level may not suit all foods and mode stirrers are already known.
Intuitive 'how hot' interface replaces time/power, though IR sensing of food temp through a cavity is imperfect and the approach is not entirely new.
Humidity sensor cooking exists in sensor-cook models, so it is feasible and helpful but not radical.
Acoustic popcorn detection exists in some products, but it is a clever, specific use that serves only one food.
Removing the start button makes operation truly two-gesture, though accidental starts with empty or unsuitable loads need safeguards.
A push-latch door is simple and cheap and removes a button, but it only addresses opening and is a minor gain.
Familiar fridge-style pull is intuitive and simple, but it only addresses opening, not the controls, and magnetic seals offer weak microwave leakage protection.
